desc:
A subarray is good if no value occurs in it more than k times. Given nums and k, return the length of the longest good subarray.

nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2], k = 2
[1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] is good (each value twice)
adding the next 1 would make it three
result = 6
hints: With k = 1 this is the classic longest subarray of distinct values. Think about how that solution generalises.
If a window is good, all of its sub-windows are good. If it is bad, any window containing it is bad.
Keep a frequency map for the window. After adding nums[right], if its count is now above k, shrink from the left until that same value's count is back to k.
editorial: Only the value that was just added can break the rule, so after extending the window to the right, check the count of nums[right]. If it exceeds k, advance left, decrementing counts, until that count drops back to k (this happens exactly when the earliest copy of that value in the window is removed).

The goodness property is hereditary (sub-windows of good windows are good), which is why the left pointer never has to retreat. Each element is added once and removed at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space for the map.
